scope: Four primary peer-reviewed sensory studies for Terroir comparison and evaluation design
retrieval_method: Non-connector scholarly web search; PubMed and Consensus were absent from available tool metadata. Crawl4AI local-first for known URLs, followed by built-in web fallback when blocked.
implementation_status: Research only. Product implications are proposals, not experimentally validated recommendation algorithms.

studies.title: Projective Mapping for interpreting wine aroma differences as perceived by naïve and experienced assessors
studies.design: Comparative sensory study: expert and consumer aroma projective mapping; expert quality and typicality; consumer liking; trained-panel descriptive analysis.

sample.wine_description: Six Tuscan PDO Sangiovese wines plus five other Italian monovarietal wines

studies.bounded_finding: Expert separation appeared mainly driven by overall quality. Consumer sample separation was clearer in liking data than in projective mapping. Descriptive-analysis and projective-mapping spaces differed.
studies.caveat: Selected high-quality Italian reds and subtle aroma differences; do not generalize to all wine styles or equate liking with sensory distance. Assessor counts unavailable in retrieved material.
studies.product_implication_inference: Keep explicit sensory resemblance labels, profile descriptions, liking, and quality judgments separate. Validate taste-similarity retrieval separately from personalized ranking.
studies.evidence_access: Publisher search-returned abstract and section snippets. Local crawler returned an IP-block/Cloudflare error page despite exit=0; treated as blocked, not full text.
studies.citation_count_source: Publisher preview; not an assessment of study quality

studies.title: Performance of Flash Profile and Napping with and without training for describing small sensory differences in a model wine
studies.design: Controlled comparison of Napping and Flash Profile protocol variants, including method/product familiarization, between-session replicates, and a within-session blind duplicate.
studies.bounded_finding: Training on either method or product improved Napping outcomes. Napping best highlighted qualitative differences; Flash Profile more precisely mapped quantitative differences in the model wines.
studies.caveat: Controlled aroma modifications in one wine base, not a heterogeneous commercial catalog. Panel size was not visible in the accessible preview.
studies.product_implication_inference: Use comparative mapping to validate broad groups and attribute-level judgments for intensity differences; check blind-duplicate agreement and repeatability.
studies.evidence_access: Publisher search-returned abstract, introduction, sample-preparation and conclusion snippets. Local crawler returned a ScienceDirect error page; built-in open returned HTTP 403.
studies.evidence_locator: Abstract; Sample preparation; Introduction objectives (a)-(d); Conclusions

studies.title: SOURNESS–SWEETNESS INTERACTIONS IN DIFFERENT MEDIA: WHITE WINE, ETHANOL AND WATER*
studies.design: Two controlled sensory mixture experiments in water and white wine, and ethanol solutions.
studies.bounded_finding: Wine mixtures elicited lower overall sourness than water and ethanol mixtures. Tartaric acid suppressed fructose sweetness more strongly than fructose suppressed tartaric-acid sourness.
studies.caveat: Nine trained assessors, specific media and tested concentrations. The study does not establish universal pH-to-sourness, titratable-acidity-to-sourness, or sugar-to-sweetness conversions.
studies.product_implication_inference: Keep perceived sweetness and sourness/tartness separate from chemistry fields and retain evidence source and measurement context.
studies.evidence_access: Local crawler failed. Built-in web retrieved publisher abstract and full bibliographic metadata, but not full experimental article.
studies.citation_count_source: Publisher CrossRef metric; not an assessment of study quality

studies.title: Oral Wine Texture Perception and Its Correlation with Instrumental Texture Features of Wine-Saliva Mixtures
studies.design: Model-wine component experiment with trained and expert sensory panels, repeated coded samples, and density/rheology tests with and without saliva.
studies.bounded_finding: The study scored body, astringency, alcoholic feeling, and bitter taste separately. Its trained-panel definition of astringency was oral dryness. Panels differed in body judgments. Viscosity did not significantly correlate with perceived body; at 100 s^-1 it correlated with astringency (r=0.855, p=0.030).
studies.caveat: Only six model formulations and one saliva donor for instrumental tests. The authors call for commercial-wine and consumer studies. Correlations are not a validated taste-prediction model.
studies.product_implication_inference: Retain distinct mouthfeel/body, mouth-drying astringency, bitterness and alcohol-warmth dimensions. Together with source 3, motivates a separate sweetness (dry-sweet) field. Capture source/panel/context instead of treating one chemical proxy as the sensory truth.
studies.evidence_access: Full publisher text retrieved by Crawl4AI; PMC fallback blocked by browser check. Built-in MDPI open returned 429 after local retrieval succeeded.
